if she examined herself every twilight... she need not be concerned for zivah. For an interruption of purity at twilight divides between the days with regard to seeing stains (as below halakhah 15), and they do not combine to be consecutive.
even though the stain is not enough for three stains. Nevertheless we suspect that she saw zivah blood on those three days.
this is a doubtful zavah. For a woman does not become a certain zavah through a stain, even if on the other two days there were definite sightings.
attributes her stain to her sighting. For only the sighting counts regarding zivah, not the stain.
within twenty-four hours. If she saw blood within a day of seeing the stain (as will be illustrated below 16-18).
she does not attribute a stain to a stain. And the first stain is regarded as a separate sighting.
Friday in the first hour of the day. On Friday, in the first hour in the morning.
until the first hour of the Sabbath day. Which is within twenty-four hours after seeing the stain.
she attributes the stain to the sighting. We do not count the day of the stain as a day of zivah, but count from the day of the sighting.
on the Sabbath in the second hour. That is, more than twenty-four hours after seeing the stain.
impure two days. Which count as two days of flow.
is concerned for zivah. And she becomes a doubtful zavah.
she saw another stain. That she saw a stain on Friday, and on the Sabbath saw another stain after it, within twenty-four hours.
counts. Her days of zivah.
she is impure two days. And counts both as days of flow.
after a full day. Specifically, for if she saw on Sunday before the full day of the stain, she attributes the Sabbath stain to the Sunday sighting, and the Sabbath is not counted as a day of zivah.
if purity intervened between them. As with stain and stain, in the previous halakhah.
she has something to attribute it to. A possibility to assume the blood's source is something else (see below halakhah 20).

for the Sages said in the matter only to be lenient, not to be stringent. For the impurity of stains is rabbinic (above halakhah 2), and therefore we are lenient with it where it can be attributed, and not stringent.
on her flesh its doubt is impure. For it is reasonable that it did not come from elsewhere but from her body (see below halakhah 21).

and if she had something to attribute it to on her flesh more than on her garment. For if it is more reasonable that the blood came from elsewhere on her body, we attribute it to that too (see below halakhah 22).
she slaughtered an animal etc.. And one should attribute it to blood that splashed on her clothes.
who was engaged with stains. She worked with garments stained with blood.
in the butchers' market. A place where animals are slaughtered.
even from the belt and above she is impure. Unlike a stain found on the garment above the belt, where she is pure (above halakhah 10), for there the stain might have come from outside.
a wound. A sore.
that healed. Was cured and does not bleed.
to open and emit blood. To open again.
on her garment and her flesh as one. And then the stain might have come from outside, and she can attribute it to things there (compare above halakhah 21).
a louse. A louse.
up to a gris. Its size was explained above halakhah 6.
more than a gris she does not attribute to a louse. For certainly such an amount is not from the louse.

and even if a louse was crushed in the stain etc.. And even if a louse was crushed in the stain and it seems that the blood is from it, nevertheless we do not attribute it to it if the size of the stain is more than a gris.
from place to place. From a certain place in the body that has blood, to another place.
on one bird. On a bird that was slaughtered.
and it has only a sela of blood. For all the blood that comes out of a bird creates a stain the size of a sela.
both are impure. For we cannot attribute it to the bird's blood, since a lot of other blood was found besides it.
attributes a gris to the blood she was engaged with and a gris to a louse. The blood that was added she attributes to the louse, up to a gris.
she was engaged with red, she does not attribute black to it. Because they are not similar to each other, although both are impure bloods (above 5:7).
many kinds. Several colors of blood.
robes. Robes.
if she can attribute it. If there was an event to which it can be attributed, such as walking in the butchers' market, as below.
attributes it to the butchers' blood. For the robes might shift, and blood from outside might splash onto the lower one.
even though the stain was found on the upper one alone she is impure. For it is reasonable that it is from her body, since she has nothing to attribute it to.
or that they come to her constantly. For the pigs wander there, even though they are not from the same place.
we are not concerned for her stains. For pigs are dirty with mud and blood, and we attribute the stains to them.
attributes it to the niddah who wore it. For a niddah is presumed to see blood, and she attributes that the stain came from her.
she attributes it to it. For they too are presumed to be seeing.
on the day of watching... in the seven clean days. For blood is presumed removed on these days (above 8:9).
both are spoiled. And each is concerned that perhaps the stain came from her.
to one who sits on the stain. A woman who saw a stain and became impure because of it.
for one does not attribute a stain to a stain. For one who sees a stain is not presumed to see blood.
the borrower is impure. For certainly the stain came from her, since she cannot attribute it to the lender.
tall. Tall.
short. Short.
if it reaches opposite her private parts. If the stain is located opposite the private parts of the tall one.
and if not, pure. If the stain is higher, it is reasonable that it came from the short one.
all are impure. For with regard to each of them there is concern that it came from her.
the two are pure. For we attribute the stain to the woman who found herself impure.
and found themselves pure. And the doubt returned regarding each of them.
a pregnant woman... a nursing woman... an old woman... a virgin. All four are removed from blood (above halakhah 4).
all of them are impure. For the doubt is equal, and it certainly came from one of them.
by the foot of the bed. The foot side, where each lay in her place and did not pass through the place of the others.
under the middle one, all three are impure. For those at her sides are close to her, and it is possible that the blood came from them.
the inner one. The one closest to the wall.
the outer one. The one farthest from the wall.
if they did not climb up by the foot of the bed. But from the outer side, and even the inner one passed through the place of the outer one.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 33.
that it be known that it is blood. That it be clear that it is blood, and not something else (see also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav uMoshav 4:11).
soaps. Cleaning agents.
in order. In sequence.
its color faded. Its color lightened.
it stood as it was. It did not change despite the washing.
fasting spittle etc.. Will be explained below halakhah 38.
natron, borit, qimonya and ashlag. Washing materials produced from various plants.
to rub. To rub the garment between his hands, as one does when washing.
with each and every agent. With each of the cleaning agents.
and moves it back and forth. Rubs back and forth.
not in order. Not according to the sequence stated above.
as one. All the signs together.
did not do anything. It does not help for clarification.
those that he applied last, which are the first ones, count etc.. Those materials are counted, and he completes the rest after them.
the next day before he eats. The spittle in his mouth the next morning is fasting spittle, provided he did not eat.
that most of his speech did not go out until three hours. That he did not speak in the amount a person speaks in this time.
and repeated his lesson. Studied by speaking.
cancels the strength of the spittle and returns it to being like water. Removes the power of the spittle to clean garments, and turns it into something like water.
the grissin. Of fava beans.
and she sits on it seven. Which are the seven days of her impurity, as for a niddah (above 4:2).
that was explained in this chapter. Above 12-18.
as we have explained. Above 5:2.
lashes for rebellion. Lashes for one who violates the words of the Sages.
and exempt from an offering. For a sin offering is brought only for Torah prohibitions.
impure like a niddah. And they are punished with karet for having relations with her (above 4:1-2).
and even if she did not see blood. Even if she did not see blood at the time of birth, for the birth itself makes her impure.
sits for a male. Impure for seven days.
sits for a female. For fourteen days.
that its form be completed. That the newborn have the form of a child, as will be explained below.
within forty days. Less than forty days from when she conceived.
she is a doubtful woman who has given birth. For after forty days it is possible that its form was completed, but there is no certainty about this.
and she sits for a male, a female, and a niddah. She is stringent to be concerned for all possibilities of impurity, of each of the events (and see in detail below halakhah 21).
extremely thin. Faint but visible.
clearly. Plainly.
she sits for a male and a female. For she certainly gave birth, and is not in doubt of niddah.
what is a formed sac. What is defined as a formed sac.
its body like a lentil. The size of a small lentil.
fly drops. Fly eyes.
its nostrils. Nostrils of the nose.
and it has no separation of hands and feet. They are not yet distinguished from its body.
became clearer. Became more distinct.
for the oil brightens it. They anoint it with oil, so that it is easier to distinguish its kind.
and moves in that place. Moves the splinter back and forth in the area of the genitals.
entangled. Meets something that prevents it from moving freely.
it is known that it is male. And the sexual organ is what blocks it.
like a split barley grain. A crack such as runs along the whole length of a barley grain.
and she does not need examination. With a splinter.
days of purity. A period after the impurity of birth in which any blood she sees is pure (above 4:5).
we do not give her days of purity. For regarding days of purity they are stringent.
that the child have hair. That there be hair on its head.
a white piece. A piece of flesh without defined form.
and a bone was found in it, she is impure. For the bone in it proves that it is a child.
a sac. A body of flesh.
geninim. Flesh cut like worms.
and it is not formed. The human form is not recognizable in it.
one who is born through the side. A child taken out through the abdominal wall, and not through the opening of the womb (caesarean section).
from the place where she conceives. The sexual organ, through which the seed enters.
the one in hardship. Who suffered before her birth and saw blood (see above 7:1).

blood of hardship that comes through the womb is zivah or niddah. Blood that comes out through the opening of the womb as usual has the law according to the days she is in, and even if it comes in the days of her zivah it does not become pure like blood of hardship (see there), because it was not followed by a regular birth.
and blood that comes through the side is impure. For the blood comes from the source, and is impure with the impurity of niddah blood (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav uMoshav 1:9).
a wound. Blood.
the child was cut up in her intestines. While inside the womb.
and came out limb by limb. And not all at once.
until most of it comes out. Most of its body, and then it is considered that she gave birth.
its whole head at once. In its entirety.
its forehead. Its forehead.
and even though it was cut up afterward. And most of the body did not come out.
impure with birth impurity by the decree of the scribes. They enacted that she become impure in this case, which is the beginning of birth.
as we have explained. In the previous halakhah.
a kind of domesticated animal, wild animal or bird. A newborn resembling these animals.
its face like the face of a person. That its face resembled a person, and not an animal.
and if its face is not in the shape of a person's face. But in the shape of an animal, as will be explained below.
and the eyebrows. The eyebrows.
and the jaws. The jawbones.
and the cheeks of the beard. The cheekbones.
the likeness of a snake. A newborn made in the shape of a snake.
that its eyeball is round like a person's. For there is a certain similarity between a snake and a person in this.
from the side. On one side of the body.
in the middle. In the center of the body.
its gullet is blocked. Sealed.
or if it lacked from its navel down and it is blocked. It lacked its entire lower half.
or if its skull was blocked. It lacked the upper part of its head.
its face is smooth. Flat.
two backs and two spines. A double back.
a creation of a head that is not cut or a hand that is not cut. A form that looks like a complete limb, except that it is not developed in the normal way.
a cut hand and a cut foot. Developed and divided in the normal way in the shaping of the fingers.
and they combine to most of its limbs. When most of its limbs came out (above halakhah 6).
sometimes the rest of the blood from which the person was formed congeals. Sometimes the excess blood in the womb congeals after the formation of the fetus.
it is not called a sandal. But it is treated like an ordinary piece, see above halakhah 4.
and the fetus will be ruined. One of the fetuses will be damaged and spoiled.
and sometimes the child dries up and changes. As a result of the blow the mother received.
and they were stringent to make her impure because of it as a child. For by strict law anything without a face form is not a child (above halakhah 3).
the thick wrapping that is like a skin bag. The thick covering that resembles a leather sack.
and the beginning of its creation resembles a weft thread. At the start of the pregnancy it is as thick as a thin weaving thread.
like a trumpet. Like a trumpet.
a woman who miscarries a placenta sits for a male and a female. Although no child was seen to be there, she must be stringent.
for there is no placenta without a child. And we assume there was a child in it that dissolved.
we are concerned for the placenta and it is like another child. That she sits for a male and a female from the time of the birth of the placenta.
we attribute it to the child. And the birth of the placenta is not considered another birth.
for the child tore the placenta and came out. For so it is reasonable, and it stayed in the womb a considerable time afterward.
for it is not the way of a placenta to come out before the child. And if it came out before it, it is understood that it belongs to another child.
they count for her from the first day. The days of her birth impurity.
and we give her days of purity only from the second day, to be stringent. For we subtract a day from the days of purity.
and a placenta tied to it. Attached to the stillborn.
we are not concerned for a child. For certainly the placenta was formed with this stillborn that has no human form, and there was no other child there that dissolved.

they impose on them the stringency of two children etc.. We are concerned that there were two fetuses: the one that was with the placenta and dissolved was in human form, and makes her impure, while the placenta of the second, which was not of human form, dissolved.
we do not give them days of purity. For this is only a concern, and not a certain birth.
that she miscarried something that is not a child etc.. That she does not become impure with birth impurity because of it.
she sits for a female. For the days of impurity and purity of a male are included in those of a female.

she sits for a male and a female. Fourteen days of impurity as for a female, and she has days of purity only up to forty days as for a male, lest she did not give birth to a female (and see below halakhah 20).
one is a female... she sits for a female only. For she certainly gave birth to a female, and has the days of purity of a female.
for a tumtum and an androgynos are doubtful. See Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25.
who was presumed pregnant. It was known that she was pregnant.
who crossed the river and miscarried there. And the stillborn was not found.
in a presumption that she miscarried a child. And she is not concerned for a stillborn that is not a child, and therefore she does not sit as a niddah.
and she sits for a male, a female and a niddah. And she has no days of purity at all, as explained below halakhah 21.
the first seven are certain. For she is impure in them whether she gave birth to a male or to a female.
up to forty days like one who gave birth to a male. Lest she gave birth to a male, and the days of purity ended.
as we have explained. Above 6:4-6.
she saw blood on the eighty-first day only. For one day, and she had seen before that after forty days were completed.

this is a doubtful niddah. For if she gave birth to a female, on this day the days of her niddah begin, but if she gave birth to a male, the days of her niddah began when she saw after completing forty days, and now she is in her days of zivah.
for she has no niddah cycle until after the completion. For the cycle of the days of niddah is fixed anew only by a sighting after forty days for a male and eighty for a female.
as we have explained. Above 6:6, 7:12.
she will be forbidden to her husband for fourteen days like one who gave birth to a female. Whereas one who gave birth to a male and a niddah are impure only seven.

she saw blood on the eighty-first day, this is a doubtful niddah. For if she gave birth to a female, her days of niddah began anew now, but perhaps she did not give birth to a female and is in the days of zivah.

she saw blood on the seventy-fourth day and on the eighty-first day, this is a doubtful niddah. She saw blood on both days, for if she gave birth to a male, her days of niddah began on the seventy-fourth day, and on the eighty-first day her days of zivah began. But it is possible that she gave birth to a female and on the eighty-first day her days of niddah began.

she saw blood on the forty-first day, even if she saw on the thirty-fourth day, this is a doubtful niddah etc.. She saw on both days, for if she gave birth to a male the days of her niddah begin on the forty-first day (and she becomes pure on the night of the forty-eighth), but it is possible that she did not give birth at all and the thirty-fourth day is of her days of niddah so that the forty-first day is of her days of zivah.
and we do not give her days of purity at all. For any blood she sees is impure, lest she did not give birth at all.
if it came in the days of her niddah. According to the cycle fixed before her birth.

a doubtful niddah after the seven from the day she miscarried. For if she saw blood within the seven days after the miscarriage she is certainly impure, either as one who gave birth or as a niddah, but afterward she is a doubtful niddah: if she did not give birth she is in the days of her niddah, and if she gave birth she is not impure until the end of the days of completion.
for all the days of completion have no cycle. Neither for days of niddah nor for days of zivah, and therefore she is a doubtful niddah or a doubtful zavah.
she is still spoiled. For she does not know whether they are the days of niddah.
as we have explained. Above in this halakhah.

and when a cycle is fixed for her after the eighty, her spoilage will depart. For then she can begin to count days of niddah and zivah anew, similar to the law of the openings of niddah (above 8:16-22).
from the day she miscarried... she is a certain niddah. Even in this case she is certainly impure, either as one who gave birth or as a niddah.
as we have explained. Above 6:2-6, the manner of fixing the days of niddah and zivah.
the law of the Torah. The law as it is at its foundation.
when the Great Court was present. When the central Sanhedrin was functioning (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:12).
great sages who recognize the bloods. Who know how to distinguish between pure and impure appearances (above 5:7-12).
would go up to the court and ask, as the Torah promised etc.. For this is what Israel did in every case of doubt or dispute in halakhah (Hilchot Mamrim 1:4).

if a matter is too hard for you etc.. If some halakhah is unclear, one must go to the Great Court, as the next verse says: "you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who will be in those days, and inquire, and they shall tell you the word of judgment."
between blood and blood, between niddah blood and zavah blood. For distinguishing between niddah and zavah bloods is among the functions of the Great Court.
and they watch their cycles. They are careful about the counting of days.
the daughter saw blood on the day of birth. On the day she was born, and then there is a need to keep up this calculation for a long time.
as we have said. Above 4:1.
but a ten-day-old. And from that day on it is possible that she will become impure with zivah, if she saw on the day she was born.
all her days. Unless the birth interrupted (above 6:4-6).
the matter became very doubtful in seeing bloods. For even then there were great sages who found it hard to distinguish between impure and pure blood (see Bavli Niddah 20b).

and the cycles became spoiled because not all women had the strength etc.. There was confusion and it was not clear which days the woman was in, because not all had the ability to follow the order of days constantly.

and they decreed that all of a woman's days be like the days of her zivah. That besides the need to count seven days whenever she sees, out of concern that she is in the days of niddah, if she saw three days she is concerned for zivah and must count seven clean days after the day she saw.
any blood she sees. Any appearance of blood, and not only the five bloods explicitly listed above 5:7-8 (see below halakhah 13).
doubtful zivah blood. See above 6:23.
and the daughters of Israel were further stringent upon themselves. In addition to what the Sages were stringent.
and all practiced it everywhere there are Israelites. This is not a stringency of a particular place, but was accepted by the whole community.

even if she saw only a drop like a mustard seed and the blood stopped etc.. That even if she saw a small amount of blood in a single sighting, they were stringent to consider her a zavah who must sit seven clean days.
and even if she saw at the time of her niddah. For by law she does not need seven clean days (above 6:2).
one day or two. For even in the days of zivah she is not a zavah, but watches a day for a day (above 6:7).
and immerses on the eighth night. Like a niddah who immerses at night (above 4:6-7).
if there was hardship. A necessity justifying immersion by day.
as we have said. Above 4:8.
within the days of completion. Until forty days for a male birth and eighty for a female, which are the days of blood of purity.
and we do not give her days of purity. For they consider the blood in these days impure.
blood of hardship. Blood that comes from labor pains, which does not defile as zivah if she gave birth (above 7:1).
like one who gives birth with a flow. For she is impure even as a zavah (see above 7:1-8).
as we have explained. Above 7:5.
and a widespread custom. Common and accepted among the public.
in Shinar. Babylonia.
and in the Land of the Gazelle. The Land of Israel.
and in the Maghreb. The countries of northwest Africa.
and this law was introduced in the days of the Geonim. The stringency of making even blood of purity impure is a practice from the time after the close of the Talmud.

for the stringency the daughters of Israel took upon themselves etc.. The stringency of requiring seven clean days even for one who sees a small amount of blood (above halakhah 4) applied only to impure blood.
blood that she sees in the days of purity after counting and immersion. Of the days of impurity of a woman who gave birth.

there is no need to be concerned for it, since the days of purity are not suitable etc.. There is no concern for error in these days, and therefore the stringency of the daughters of Israel does not apply to this situation, and their prohibition is only from the custom of the Geonim.
as we have explained. Above 4:5.
and we have heard that in France they have relations during blood of purity according to the law of the Talmud to this day. That they were not stringent there to make blood of purity impure.
and this matter depends on custom. For this stringency did not spread to all Jewish communities, and depends on local custom.
and likewise the law of hymen blood. Although by strict law it is pure, since it is not from the source but like blood of a wound (above 5:18).
for even if she was a minor. For by law she is permitted to her husband until the wound heals (ibid.).
has relations the mitzvah relations and withdraws. After the first intercourse he separates from her (see above 5:19).
and as long as she sees blood from the wound. From the wound from which the hymen blood comes.
seven clean days. As if she had seen impure blood.
that they asked her to marry and she agreed. That they requested her to marry, and she consented.
since she agreed. She counts seven from the day after her consent.
from her desire for the man. From her wish and longing for the husband.
an extra stringency that the daughters of Israel practiced. A stringency added on top of the basic law.
and one may never depart from it. The halakhah must not be changed and relaxed in this matter (see Hilchot Mamrim 2:3).
that she agreed when they asked her to marry. That she agreed when she was asked to marry.
and she counts from after she married. She counts the seven clean days after the marriage.
and he does not approach her until she immerses. Like a niddah, where we rely on a Torah scholar not to come to rule leniently against the halakhah.
as we have explained. Above chapter 9.
and there is no innovation or custom in the matter. For with stains the daughters of Israel did not adopt the stringency they adopted with seeing blood as mentioned above halakhah 4.

counts seven clean days from the day the stain was found. She acts like a niddah who needs seven days beginning that day (and these days must be clean, for if she sees in them she will need to count seven days anew, out of concern that the days of niddah are only now beginning; see above halakhah 3).

if the measure of the stain was enough to be concerned for zivah, she counts seven days from after the day the stain was found. For if the stain was enough for three sightings, she is concerned for zivah even with stains, and needs seven clean days after the day of the sighting (see above 9:12).
for one who sees blood is not like one who sees a stain. For the impurity of stains is by rabbinic decree (above 9:2).
whose mother is pure. Who is not impure because of the birth, such as one who miscarried a child whose form was not complete (above 10:1), or whose face was like that of an animal (above 10:8-9).
who saw white or green blood. Pure appearances (above 5:6).
who discharged a red piece with no blood. That she miscarried a piece, even though it is red (above 5:13).
and likewise if she had a wound and the blood was dripping from it. If she had a sore in the womb and the blood flowed from it.
or the blood came with urine. She found blood in urine.
this is pure. For it is only blood of a wound, and pure (above 5:17).
for anyone who sees impure blood, as we have said. Above halakhah 6.
and that all appearances of blood be impure. They were stringent to make impure every appearance containing redness, even if it is not one of the five impure bloods (above 5:7-12).
this that you will find in some places. If you see that they practice in this manner, which is not the custom of the majority.
sits seven days in her niddah etc.. That she does not count seven clean days until seven days have passed from the beginning of the sighting.

it is an error on the part of whoever ruled for them. For if she does not see blood in the days of her niddah, the days count for her toward the seven clean days even if she is a full zavah (see above 7:6).
the second night after the days of her niddah. For she added one day to her days of niddah, to complete seven clean days, and immerses at night.
and likewise this that you will find in some places and you will find responsa of some Geonim etc.. What was practiced in certain places on the basis of rulings of earlier sages.
she shall not have relations until the end of forty etc.. For the whole time of blood of purity is forbidden, even if she did not see blood in it.
those responsa are an error. For from the standpoint of halakhah there is no reason to forbid her, if she did not see blood at all.
and in the manner of heresy etc.. For according to those who deny the Sages' tradition, there is no time of blood of purity, and these are days of impurity even without blood.
and it is a mitzvah to compel them in order to remove it from their hearts. To instruct them firmly not to practice thus, so that they will not think this is the law.
as we have explained. Above halakhot 5-7.
comes up from her impurity and leaves the status of a forbidden relation. She becomes pure, and the karet prohibition of having relations with her is lifted.
in the water of a valid mikveh. Which has forty se'ah of water that is not drawn.
interposes. Separates.
and in Hilchot Mikva'ot the valid and invalid mikveh will be explained. Chapter 4.
and the manner of immersion. 1:7-12.
and the laws of interposition. Chapter 2.
but if she bathed in a bathhouse. In a bathhouse, a place of washing that is not a valid mikveh.
even if all the waters of the world fell on her she is after the washing as she was. For such washing does not help her purification at all, even with a large quantity of water.
a mikveh. A collection of rainwater.
in a spring. A flow of water from the ground.
in the seas. In the sea.
as will be explained in Hilchot Mikva'ot. 9:12.
as if no immersion had come up for her. The immersion does not count, because they are like the seven clean days of a zavah, in which immersion does not help (above 6:12).
and if she immersed on the seventh. By day, which is the ideal time of immersion for a major zavah (above 6:11).

for it is forbidden to do so in the first place, lest he come to have relations on the seventh after the immersion. For this time is in doubt, since she may see blood after the immersion and cancel the clean days, and be found impure retroactively (above 6:13-14).

since she immersed at her time, even if she was a certain zavah. For even if we were stringent to consider her a major zavah and require seven clean days, she immersed at the proper time for immersion.
that he cling to his wife. That they sleep together.
she in her garment and he in his garment. Both dressed in their clothes.
he should approach. Come near.

he should behave with her in the days of counting as he behaves in the days of niddah. They should act with the prohibition in the seven clean days as in the days of niddah, for in practice there is no difference between the days of counting and the days of niddah.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 16.
all the work that a wife does for her husband. To help with the livelihood, to serve her husband, and various tasks needed for life at home, such as cooking and laundry (see Hilchot Ishut 21:1-7).
except for washing his face, hands and feet etc.. For these bring about closeness (see also ibid. 21:8).
and mixing the cup. Preparing wine in a cup for drinking, and diluting it with water.
in one bowl. From the same dish.
because of the habit of transgression. For they might come to forbidden intercourse.
to adorn herself in the days of her niddah. With makeup or fine clothes.
she will become repulsive. She will become loathsome.
in a marital way. Within married life.

whether the seven nations or all the nations in this prohibition. The prohibition applies both to the nations that lived in the land of Canaan when Israel conquered it, and to the other peoples of the world.

and so it is explicit through Ezra. In the covenant signed by the people under the leadership of Ezra and Nehemiah, in which they committed to keep and do all the commandments of the Torah. And there it states explicitly that all foreign peoples are included in the prohibition of intermarriage.
by way of intermarriage. A marriage bond.
by way of fornication. Without marriage.
designated her for himself. A permanent relationship.
because of a niddah, a maidservant etc.. For the Sages enacted that he receive lashes because of these four transgressions.
by chance. Occasionally.
by their decree. By rabbinic decree.

a priest who has relations with a gentile woman receives lashes from the Torah as one who marries a zonah. For it is forbidden to him by the Torah to marry a zonah (for the definition of a zonah forbidden to the priesthood see below 18:1).
both a gentile zonah and an Israelite zonah. For the verse made no distinction in their prohibition, and both are forbidden to him (see also below 17:6).
and for intercourse alone he is lashed. In contrast to forbidden Israelite women, where he is lashed only if he betrothed and had relations (below 17:2).
is not subject to betrothal. For betrothal does not take effect with gentiles (Hilchot Ishut 4:15, Hilchot Gerushin 10:19).
if he had relations with her publicly. In front of many.
before ten Israelites. For there is a desecration of God's name in this (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:4).
if zealots attacked him. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:6.
praiseworthy and diligent. For they did a proper deed.
and proof of this is the deed of Phinehas with Zimri. For Zimri had relations with a Midianite woman in front of all Israel, and Phinehas killed both of them (see Numbers 25:1-15).
but only at the time of the act, like Zimri. Only at the time of intercourse, as in that incident.

and the woman through her belly. For Phinehas struck Zimri and the woman with a spear in her belly or her private parts, from which it follows that Zimri did not separate from her at the time she was killed.

but if he separated, we do not kill him, and if he killed him, he is killed for it. If the man separated from the woman it is forbidden to kill him, and if the zealot killed him anyway, the zealot is judged as a murderer and liable to death.

and if the zealot came to take permission from the court to kill him, we do not instruct him etc.. If he asks the court's approval, they do not permit him to kill, for the man has no death penalty by law.
and the man slipped away and killed the zealot... the man is not killed for it. For he is permitted to save himself like any pursued person (Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:6).

the daughter of a resident alien. The daughter of a gentile resident in the Land of Israel who accepted upon himself to keep the seven Noahide commandments, and especially not to worship idols (see below 14:7).
his punishment is explicit in the words of the Prophets that he is cut off. It is stated explicitly in the words of the Prophets that his punishment is karet.
he shall have none who wakes among the sages nor one who answers among the students. That he will not be able to learn and expound among the sages, nor even to answer those who ask.
who brings an offering to the Lord of Hosts. A priest serving in the Temple.
and he is called one who profanes the holy. The sanctity of the people of Israel.
even though it has no court-imposed death. And therefore it might seem that it is not so severe.
it has a loss that no other forbidden relations have. There is in it a deficiency and damage greater than in the transgression of other forbidden relations.
and he is counted among Israel even though he is a mamzer. For his law is that of a Jew.
and the son from the gentile woman is not his son. He is not attributed to him for any matter of halakhah (see Hilchot Yibbum vaChalitzah 1:4, Hilchot Nachalot 2:12, Hilchot Mamrim 5:9).
turns him away from following the Lord. For one who intermarries with gentiles causes his son to no longer be counted in the congregation of the Lord.
and this matter. The sin of intercourse with a gentile woman.
and to turn away from following the Lord and to commit a trespass against Him. For it causes him to worship idols.
if she is a married woman he is killed for her. For a married woman is forbidden even to a gentile (Hilchot Melachim 9:7, 10:5).
and if she is unmarried he is not killed. For she is not a forbidden relation.
a minor girl three years and a day old. Who is fit for intercourse (above 1:13).
for a stumbling block came to Israel through her, like the animal. Just as an animal is stoned if a person has relations with it (above 1:16-18).
these were to the children of Israel in the matter of Balaam. Since the daughters of Midian caused many of Israel to stumble (in the incident of Zimri), they were sentenced to death.
the slaves whom they immersed for the sake of slavery. For this is the law of the slaves of Israel (see below 13:11-12, 14:9).

and they accepted upon themselves the commandments that slaves are obligated in. Slaves are obligated in the commandments, and exempt from those commandments from which women are exempt (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).
they have left the category of gentiles, but have not entered the category of Israel. In halachic terms they are in an intermediate status (and see below 14:17).
forbidden to a free man. To one who is not a slave, as she is not yet part of the Jewish people.

whether his own maidservant or the maidservant of another. Both are forbidden, since we cannot assume that a man who refrains from a forbidden relation would have freed his maidservant before being with her (see on this Hilchot Gerushin 10:19, Hilchot Avadim 9:1).

for it is explicit in the Torah, etc.. From the explicit Torah permission for a Hebrew slave to be with a maidservant, it is evident that the prohibition of a maidservant to an Israelite is only rabbinic.
If his master gives him a wife. The master of a Hebrew slave may give him a Canaanite maidservant as a wife (see also Hilchot Avadim 3:3).
and the Sages did not decree in this matter. A prohibition against a Hebrew slave marrying a maidservant.
a designated maidservant. One who is half freed and betrothed to a Hebrew slave.
as we have explained. Above 3:13-14.
this sin. Relations with a maidservant.
for this too causes the son to turn away from following the Lord. Like relations with a gentile woman (above halachah 7).

for the son of a maidservant is a slave and not an Israelite. For we follow the mother, and he has the full status of a slave (see below 15:4, Hilchot Yibbum VaChalitzah 1:4, Hilchot Avadim 9:1, Hilchot Nachalot 2:12, Hilchot Mamrim 5:11).
Onkelos the translator. Who translated the Torah into Aramaic, according to the tradition of the Sages.

he included relations with a slave and a maidservant, etc.. According to the Targum, this prohibition derives from the meaning of the verse (although in practice the verse is expounded as referring to the prohibition of a prostitute; see Hilchot Ishut 1:4).
and at the time of the transgression. During the act itself.
zealots may not strike him. Unlike with a gentile woman (above halachah 4).
he does not receive lashes from the Torah. Unlike with a gentile woman (above halachah 1).
she has left the category of gentiles. She is not considered a gentile (above halachah 11).
the child of an Israelite woman became mixed up with the child of a maidservant. So that it is not known which was born to whom.

and we compel the maidservant's owner to free both of them. For while they are of uncertain slave status, they are forbidden to marry either a maidservant or a free woman, and are barred from procreation (see Hilchot Avadim 7:7).
and if the son was the master of the slave. One of the mixed-up children was the master of the other child.
when they grow up. For a minor cannot free his slave (and see there 7:8).
they free one another. For each of them is the owner of the other.
and they are permitted to enter the congregation of the Lord. To marry an Israelite woman.
of uncertain conversion. And she is forbidden to a kohen (below 18:3, 19:9).
all the nations. People of every nation.
they are like Israelites in every respect. With regard to their obligation in the commandments.
to enter the congregation of the Lord. With regard to marriage.
except for four nations only. Four nations whose converts have limited possibilities for marriage with Israelites, as will be explained below in halachot 18-21.
except with regard to marrying into the congregation. That is, except for the possibility of marrying Israelites, though they may marry other converts (see below 15:7).
forbidden with a permanent prohibition, the males. Even if they convert, they are forbidden to marry Israelite women, under a negative commandment (Hilchot Ishut 1:7).
until the end of the world. All generations.

the first generation and the second generation are forbidden to enter Israel. An Egyptian or Edomite who converted, and the children born to them after their conversion, are forbidden to marry an Israelite man or woman; this is a prohibition from a positive commandment (Hilchot Ishut 1:8).
and the third generation is permitted. The grandchild of an Egyptian or Edomite convert.
a pregnant Egyptian woman who converted, her son is second generation. For the son is not a convert but was born with Jewish holiness (see below 13:7).
who are born to them, the verse tied it to birth. From the verse we learn that the son born must be third generation to both of them, father and mother.
the child is Ammonite. And is forbidden to enter the congregation.
the child is Egyptian. A second-generation Egyptian, and the generation after will be fit to enter the congregation.
among the nations we follow the male. When they are gentiles, nationality is determined by the father (see below 15:6).
if they converted, we follow the lesser one. The parent whose defect is more severe.
from the seven nations. From the nations that lived in the land of Canaan when Israel conquered it.
they are not forbidden by the Torah to enter the congregation. For the prohibition of intermarriage with them applies only while they are gentiles, as with the other nations (above halachah 1).

and it is known that only the Gibeonites converted from them. The book of Joshua (9:3-27) relates that the Gibeonites deceived the Israelites and made a peace covenant with them, which implies that they converted.

and woodcutters and water drawers... he tied their distancing to the Temple. Because they became servants of the Temple, there is a connection between the existence of the Temple and the decree of prohibition.
and they are called Nethinim. The Gibeonite converts were called Nethinim, because they were given over to the Temple service.
that they would never enter the congregation, etc.. That they would be forbidden to marry Israelites in all generations.
whom David and the princes gave for the service of the Levites. This implies that David decreed that they be assigned to serve the Levites, even when there is no Temple.
the brazenness and cruelty that was in them. And he held that for this reason they are unfit to mix with Israel (see below 19:17).
when the seven sons of Saul were requested... and they killed them. In revenge for Saul having killed some of the Gibeonites (see II Samuel 21:1-14).
he mixed up all the nations. He exiled peoples from their places and replaced them with others.
they are other people. Not the original natives of the place.
that is in the field of Edom. The land of Edom (based on Genesis 32:4).
the four forbidden nations. Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians and Edomites.

the presumption is that he separated from the majority. If one individual came out of a mixture, he is presumed to be from the majority, and most gentiles are not forbidden (for this rule see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:11).
at this time. That is, after the time of Sennacherib.
everywhere. Even in the land of Egypt, Edom, etc.
permitted to enter the congregation immediately. And there is no concern that they came from the forbidden nations.
Israel entered the covenant. The covenant with the Holy One, blessed be He, on accepting the Torah and the commandments.
circumcision was in Egypt. The Israelites were circumcised there before the Passover offering was brought.
when it says, "and no uncircumcised person...". Since eating the Egyptian Passover offering was forbidden to the uncircumcised, and at that time Moses our teacher circumcised all of Israel.
that they had all nullified the covenant of circumcision in Egypt. All the Israelites did not observe this commandment during the Egyptian exile.
and about this it says, "and they kept Your covenant". In Moses' blessing to the tribe of Levi, which testifies that they kept the covenant even when the rest were not careful.
and immersion. In a mikveh.

when it says, "and sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments". The Israelites were commanded to prepare in this way for the event at Mount Sinai; this refers to immersion and washing garments.
when it says, "and he sent the young men of the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings". After the event at Mount Sinai.
they offered them on behalf of all Israel. For all of Israel.
and so for all generations. Just as the people of Israel entered the covenant with these three things, so must a gentile who comes to convert do.
and to take shelter. To find refuge.
he requires circumcision, immersion, and the bringing of an offering. For the details of the conversion procedure see below 14:1-6.
and the bringing of an offering. Bringing an offering for acceptance.
and if she is a female. She does not need circumcision.
a burnt offering of an animal, etc.. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:6, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:2.
and at this time when there is no offering. Offerings are not brought, because the Temple is destroyed.
and he must immerse before three. Who serve as a court (below 14:6).
we do not immerse him on Shabbat, on a festival, or at night. For a court does not sit in judgment at these times (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:14, Hilchot Sanhedrin 3:3).
we immerse him on the authority of a court. For a minor has no understanding, and the court may immerse him on their own authority (see also Hilchot Melachim 10:3).
for it is to his benefit. To be a Jew; and we may act to a person's benefit even in his absence, and likewise for a minor without his consent (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:8).
her son does not require immersion. For he was already born with Jewish holiness.
by himself. Alone.
even before two, he is not a convert. For a court of three is required (above halachah 6).
to enter the congregation. To marry an Israelite woman.
until he brings witnesses. That he did in fact convert there.
he is believed to disqualify himself. To be considered a gentile on the basis of his words; and he is forbidden to his wife until he converts properly.
but he is not believed to disqualify the children. They are not considered the children of a gentile, and the daughters are fit for the priesthood (see below 19:12).
terumah from her dough. Separating challah.
who immerses for his seminal emission. To become pure from the impurity of an emission.
presumed to be righteous converts. They were presumed so because of their conduct as Israelites.
we do not marry them off until they bring witnesses. This presumption is not enough to permit them to enter the congregation, for the Sages were strict regarding lineage (see below halachah 10).
for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Since he was presumed to be a gentile only on the basis of his own words, he is believed to permit himself and say that he converted.

in the Land of Israel and in those days when everyone there is presumed to be Jewish. When the people of Israel lived in their land, and the default assumption about the inhabitants was that they were Israelites, so that anyone who came was presumed to be Jewish.
but outside the Land he must bring proof. The rule "the mouth that forbade" does not apply in this case, because even without his testimony he would be presumed a gentile.
and I say that this is a stringency regarding lineage. It seems that the requirement of proof is a special strictness in matters of lineage and marriage, and is not the essence of the law.
who circumcise. Who perform circumcision.
those acquired from gentiles. Gentile slaves purchased from gentiles (for their conversion procedure see below 14:9).
for the purpose of slavery. He immerses to accept the commandments as a slave (above 12:11).

and the slave went first and immersed for the purpose of a free man, he acquired himself. He intended conversion and not slavery, thereby became a convert and a free man, and is no longer a slave (see also Hilchot Avadim 8:19).
he immerses before you. Before the court.
he need not specify. To say explicitly that he is immersing as a free man.
rather, once he immersed he was freed. The master should have said that this immersion was for the purpose of slavery, as explained below.
to hold him tightly in the water until he comes up, while he is under his control. To grip him firmly while he is in the water, so that he does not leave his control until he comes up from there.
for it is partial conversion. A partial conversion (above 12:11).
he requires another immersion before three, in the daytime. As with a conversion (above halachah 6).
and in a mikveh fit for a menstruant's immersion. A gathering of forty se'ah of water that is not drawn (above 11:16).
and anything that interposes. Things stuck to the body that prevent the water from reaching the whole body during immersion (see Hilchot Mikva'ot chapter 2).
that Samson, the savior of Israel. Samson the mighty.
the beloved of the Lord. Another name of King Solomon (II Samuel 12:25).

married foreign women while they were still gentiles. While they were still gentile women. Regarding Samson it says, "And Samson went down to Timnah, and saw a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines" (Judges 14:1). Regarding Solomon, "And King Solomon loved many foreign women..." (I Kings 11:1).
the secret of the matter. The explanation, which is not explicit in Scripture.
that the proper commandment. The proper way.
we investigate him. We inquire into the reason he wants to convert.
money he will receive. Will earn money.
perhaps he set his eyes... she set her eyes. That they want to convert in order to marry Israelites.
a pretext. An ulterior motive for conversion.
and the burden involved in performing it upon the common people. The commandments are considered a burden by the masses.
so that they will withdraw. So that they will give up.
they accepted and did not withdraw. They agreed to take it upon themselves.
who returned. Who came to convert.
out of love. And not for any other reason.

"And she saw that she was determined to go with her, and she stopped speaking to her". After Naomi saw that Ruth insisted on staying with her, she stopped trying to persuade her to return to her land.
in the days of David, perhaps out of fear. Which he imposed on the nations through his military victories.
something of the vanities of the world. A material benefit, which is nothing but vanity.
is not one of the righteous converts. This conversion is not proper.
before laymen. Who are not a properly constituted court.
we do not push them away. From their conversion, since their conversion was done lawfully (see below halachah 17).
and we do not draw them close. We do not treat them as righteous converts but as attached converts (see below halachah 18).
until their end is seen. Until it becomes known whether they converted for the sake of Heaven.
but for the sake of something. Another reason.
and Scripture considered them as if they were gentile women and still in their prohibition. Therefore Scripture calls them gentile women, as if they were still forbidden.
for their end proved their beginning. In the end they worshipped idols, which proves that they did not convert for the sake of Heaven in the first place.
and Scripture ascribed it to him as if he had built them. Scripture places the blame on Solomon himself, although it was the deed of the women, because he converted them improperly.
for they did not investigate him. Whether he was converting for some other reason.
until his righteousness becomes clear. To prove whether he is a righteous convert.
like an apostate Israelite. A Jew who converted to idolatry, who retains the status of an Israelite (see also Hilchot Melachim 10:3).
that his betrothals are valid betrothals. If he married a Jewish woman, the betrothal takes effect (Hilchot Ishut 4:15).
and it is a commandment to return his lost item. Whereas there is no commandment to return a gentile's lost item (Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 11:3).
once he has immersed he has become like an Israelite. Despite the deficiencies in this conversion.

and therefore Samson and Solomon kept their wives. And did not divorce them, even though it became clear that they had not converted for the sake of Heaven, since they had become Israelites in any case.
the mixed multitude. The converts who left Egypt with the Israelites and incited them to complain about the conditions in the wilderness (see Numbers 11:4).
for most return for some reason. They come to convert for various reasons, not for the sake of Heaven.
to separate from them. To keep apart from them.
in the incident of the calf. Exodus chapter 32.
and at Kivrot HaTa'avah. Numbers chapter 11.
how do we accept righteous converts. How the acceptance process is conducted.
and they do not find a pretext. Another reason for which he came to convert (above 13:14).
what did you see. Why.
wasted, pushed about, driven and tossed. Weak, rejected, forced down, lowly and wandering from place to place.
I know, and I am not worthy. I know their condition, and I am not worthy of this; would that I might merit to join Israel.
the unity of the Name. Belief that the Lord alone is the creator and ruler of the world, and that His power is unlimited (Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 1:1-7).
and they elaborate on this matter. They go into detail on this, as it is a fundamental principle of the Jewish religion (see Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:2).
the sin of leket, shichechah, pe'ah and the poor tithe. The obligation to give gifts to the poor from the produce, and the sin of withholding them.
that before you came to this faith, etc.. As long as you had not converted you were not obligated in the commandments.
forbidden fat. Portions of animal fat forbidden to eat on pain of karet (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot chapter 7).
you desecrated Shabbat. By labors forbidden by the Torah, for which, if done before witnesses, one is liable to death by stoning (Hilchot Shabbat 1:2).
and they do not add to it or be exacting with him. In detailing the commandments and their punishments.
to trouble him and turn him from a good path to an evil path. So that he will regret his good desire to convert.

and so it says, "with cords of a man," etc.. At first one should speak to a person's heart gently and pleasantly ("cords of a man"), and afterwards one may also raise more severe matters without causing him to draw away ("bands of love").
with bands. Thick ropes.
and there is no completely righteous person, etc.. A completely righteous person is only one who knows the Torah well and keeps its commandments.
hidden. Stored away.
in suffering in this world. That they have many troubles.
like the nations. Like all the other peoples.
most of the calamity. Many troubles.
all the nations come to an end while they endure. The other nations vanish from the world, while the people of Israel endures.
and they elaborate on this matter in order to endear it to him. Here too they go into detail, to make Judaism dear to them.
goes on his way. And we do not convert him.
they delay. They wait.
they circumcise. They perform the circumcision.
they draw from him the blood of the covenant. They cut the site of the circumcision until blood comes out, which is a kind of covenant (see also Hilchot Milah 1:7).
and three stand. They are the court (above 13:6).
a second time. In addition to what they told him when he came to convert (above halachah 2): that in immersing he enters the yoke of the commandments and must accept them.
and he stands in the water. While he is inside the mikveh.
women seat her in the water, etc.. For reasons of modesty.
she immerses before them. And they see only the immersion of her head.
they turn their faces and leave. They turn around and go outside.

the commandments that the sons of Noah were commanded. The prohibitions of blasphemy, murder, adultery, robbery, and eating a limb from a living animal, and the commandment to establish courts (Hilchot Melachim 9:1).
we accept him, etc.. Before three Israelites who are careful in observing the commandments (there 8:10).

he is one of the righteous of the nations of the world. And he has a share in the world to come, provided that he does so because of the command of the Holy One, blessed be He; but if he observed them out of rational conviction, he is not a resident alien and is not among the righteous of the nations but among their wise men (there 8:11).
as we explained in Hilchot Avodah Zarah. 10:6.

when the Jubilee is in effect. When all the inhabitants are in the Land and each tribe is in its place. Since the exile of the two and a half tribes, the Jubilees have ceased and we do not accept a resident alien (Hilchot Shemittah VeYovel 10:8-9, Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6, Hilchot Milah 1:6, Hilchot Shabbat 20:14).
at this time. In our days.
except for one point of precision. Something the Sages learned from close study of Scripture.
one acquired from gentiles. Who was purchased from a gentile.
we do not say to him, "What did you see that you came?". As we say to a convert (above halachah 1).
of the fit ones. Slaves who behave properly.
we roll with him. We wait for him to agree to the matter.
and sells him to gentiles. If he did not agree within twelve months (see also Hilchot Milah 1:6, Hilchot Avadim 8:12).
and if he stipulated. The slave.
except at the time of the Jubilee. As with a resident alien (above halachah 7).

no relation is forbidden to them on account of incest, etc.. The definition of forbidden relations for gentiles is not the same as those forbidden to Israelites (listed above 1:4-7 and in the enumeration of commandments at the beginning of this section).
as will be explained in Hilchot Melachim UMilchamot. 9:5.

like a newborn child, and all the relatives he had when he was a gentile or a slave are no longer relatives. A convert is considered newly born, and so his closeness to his family is void (see also Hilchot Edut 13:2).
that a convert is permitted to marry his mother, etc.. For they are not considered relatives from the moment he converted.

so that they will not say they came from a stricter holiness to a lighter holiness. So that it should not appear that conversion caused prohibitions to be permitted. For the opposite is true: the holiness of Israel and its prohibitions are greater and more numerous than those of the gentiles (for another example see Hilchot Mamrim 5:11).
yesterday. Earlier, when he was a gentile.
in her gentile state. While she was a gentile.
as if he had relations with a gentile woman. A gentile woman, and he is not liable on account of incest.
what is the law of converts regarding the forbidden relations of blood relatives. According to rabbinic enactment they are forbidden even after converting.
we separate them. We keep them apart, since the closeness between them was forbidden even when they were gentiles.
as we explained. In the previous halachah.
we do not separate them. Since they converted they are not relatives, and these women were not forbidden to him before either.
on the mother's side. Relatives on the mother's side.
such as twins. Who were born of one pregnancy, and surely have one father.
his brother's wife on his father's side. Whom he married after he converted.
and his daughter who converted is permitted to him. Because he is her father, and converts have no prohibition regarding relatives on the father's side.
their conception was not in holiness but their birth was in holiness. The mother converted after becoming pregnant and before giving birth.
they are liable on account of a brother's wife. They are considered full brothers with respect to their lineage through the mother, since they were born when she was already a convert.
let him stay with one of them and divorce the other. For they are each other's maternal relatives and are forbidden to an Israelite.
for they only decreed it during their lifetimes. The prohibition of these is weakened after the woman's death, even for an Israelite (see above 2:8-9).
as we explained. Above halachah 13.
the secondary relations. Relatives forbidden by rabbinic enactment (for the list see Hilchot Ishut 1:6).
a convert is permitted to marry his mother's mother. Although she is a maternal relative, since she is not forbidden by the Torah to an Israelite.
while he is a slave. And has not been freed.
for he has already left the category of gentiles... and has not entered the category of Israel. Above 12:11.
equal for every person. And does not depend on nationality (for their prohibition see above 1:14-16; and see also Hilchot Melachim 9:5).
slaves who were freed are like converts. See also above 13:12.
in the first instance. This is not prostitution, and there is no prohibition even in the first instance.
and they do not require any "name of a thing" but are like animals. They have no legal framework of betrothal and marriage ("shem davar" means "any thing").
it is the same. This makes no difference regarding the slaves.
and not for slaves with Israelites. See Hilchot Ishut 4:15.
the mamzer mentioned in the Torah. Who is forbidden to enter the congregation of the Lord.

one born of a forbidden relation among the forbidden relations. One born of intercourse forbidden as incest (for the list see above 1:4-7 and the enumeration of commandments at the beginning of this section).
except for a menstruant, whose son is defective but is not a mamzer. His lineage has a flaw, but he is permitted to enter the congregation.
by force. Compulsion.
by mistake. Lack of knowledge.
forbidden forever. To marry fit Israelites, as are their descendants.
even the tenth generation. The continuation of the verse: "shall not enter the congregation of the Lord."
since they had relations after the betrothal they receive lashes. For the prohibition applies only to relations within marriage.
for among all those liable under negative commandments, etc.. In all of them the prohibition is by means of marriage.
as will be explained. Below 17:3.
one who remarries his divorcee after she married another. A man is forbidden to take her back after she has married someone else (Hilchot Gerushin 11:12).
for she is not a forbidden relation. She falls under negative commandments, not under those punishable by karet.
the child is fit. We disregard the gentile and the slave, and follow the mother alone (below 15:3-4).
with a married woman. The seed of the gentile is disregarded even in a forbidden union.
the child is a mamzer. For we follow the mother, and she is a mamzeret.
fit like other converts. He is not a mamzer, for there is no mamzer status among gentiles.
and he is permitted to an Israelite woman. The son who is a convert or freed slave, for his father is not considered at all.
according to this principle. According to this principle, that the father is not considered in mixed marriages.
to purify his children. To permit them to marry into Israel.
for he frees them. Those born to his maidservant are his slaves, and he can free them.
and they did not decree against a maidservant for a mamzer. Although they decreed a prohibition for an ordinary Israelite (above 12:11).
who is half slave and half free. Who belonged to two partners, and one of them freed him.
that son. The one born of them.

for an aspect of slavery and an aspect of mamzer status are mixed in him. and his children are found to be like him forever. If he married an Israelite woman or a convert.
a maidservant who immersed... and a slave who immersed. For the purpose of slavery.
follow the mother. According to the rule of the relationship between Israelite and gentile or slave (above halachot 3-4), for slaves who immersed have left the category of gentiles (above 12:11).
a gentile maidservant or a gentile slave. Who did not immerse.
follows the male. For such is the law among the nations (above 12:21).
follows the defective one. And the lineage defect of a mamzer is greater than that of a convert.
for it says, "in the congregation of the Lord". From which we learn that the marriage prohibition of a mamzer applies only with Israelites, who are called the congregation of the Lord.
he is permitted to a mamzeret. For he is still called a convert, since neither of his parents is Jewish.
whose conception and birth were in holiness. The pregnancy of that son was after the mother's conversion.
and likewise his grandson. For they are still called converts.
until the name of his being a convert is forgotten. People forget that he was a convert and consider him a full Israelite, even though his parents were converts (and see below 19:12).
freed slaves, one law for all of them. With regard to marriage with mamzerim.
an Israelite in every respect. And he is counted in the congregation of the Lord.
there are three kinds of mamzerim. Three types, whose laws are not the same.
as we explained. Above halachah 1.

who was betrothed with a doubtful betrothal, etc.. And there is doubt whether a forbidden relation exists (for examples see Hilchot Ishut 4:21-22, Hilchot Gerushin 5:13). His law will be explained below in halachot 21-24.

who heard that her husband died and married, and her husband is alive. She married another, and it turned out that the first husband had not died, and she is forbidden to both (see Hilchot Gerushin 10:5).
and her husband came to her while she was under the second. Her first husband had relations with her while she was married to the second husband.

a mamzer by rabbinic enactment. Rabbinically the woman needs a get from the second as well, and her son from the first is a mamzer, although by Torah law the second betrothal is not valid because she is a married woman (see there 10:7). His law will be explained below in halachah 22.
an unmarried woman who became pregnant through licentiousness. Intercourse without marriage canopy or betrothal.
he is fit, and it was to an Israelite that I was with. His father was fit to enter the congregation.
even though most of the city that was licentious with her are unfit. For instance, if they were mamzerim, because we rely on the mother's word regarding fitness.
or if she was deaf, etc.. And it is impossible to rely on her testimony.
or if she said. She explicitly admitted that the man was unfit.
the Nathin. See above 12:22.
a doubtful mamzer, etc.. We are concerned that he may be unfit by default, but we do not rely entirely on the mother's words so as to consider him a definite mamzer.
shetuki. From the word for silence.
asufi. Gathered from the marketplace.
for we do not know what he is. Whether he is fit for the congregation or unfit.
he is the son of so-and-so. She says she became pregnant by a certain man.
the son is fit. For we rely on her words (as above halachah 11).
and she is not believed that this is the son of so-and-so. This testimony is not accepted regarding inheritance of money or lineage.
he is forbidden to that man's relatives out of doubt. Perhaps her words are true, and that man's relatives are forbidden to the son as incest.
as we explained. Above halachah 12.
who was established as his son. It was known that this man is his son.
this son of mine is a mamzer. And unfit to enter the congregation.
he is not believed, etc.. For the Torah gives a father no credibility regarding his grandchildren, and therefore he is not believed even about his son (see also Hilchot Nachalot 4:2).
he may acknowledge him to others, etc.. He is believed to testify that he is a firstborn (see also there 2:14), and likewise is believed to testify to his lineage.
the son of a divorcee or the son of a chalutzah. Who is disqualified from the priesthood (see below 19:3, 19:8).
he is believed to say, "This fetus is not my son". But from another man, and consequently he is a mamzer.
and he shall be a definite mamzer. For the father is fully believed regarding the status of the son (compare above halachah 12).
he is believed to forbid himself to an Israelite woman. To be strict, disqualifying him from the congregation, for regarding prohibition his words are accepted.
and he is forbidden to a mamzeret. For he is not to be considered a definite mamzer on his own testimony.
and his son is like him. A doubtful mamzer, who is forbidden to a mamzeret and to an Israelite woman.
he is not believed to disqualify his grandchildren. Therefore he does not disqualify his own children either.
a betrothed woman who became pregnant while in her father's house. She was betrothed and not yet married (see Hilchot Ishut 10:1), and with regard to others she is forbidden as a married woman.
presumed a mamzer and forbidden to an Israelite woman. We assume she became pregnant from others, so the fetus is a mamzer.
and forbidden to a mamzeret. For it is possible that she became pregnant from her betrothed, and the fetus is fit.
his mother was examined and said, "I became pregnant by my betrothed," she is believed and the child is fit. Like an unmarried woman who was with a fit man (above halachah 14).
for even if he had been presumed to be his son... he is believed. As in halachot 15-16 above, and certainly he is believed before he was established as his son.
she is not presumed a prostitute. That she would be forbidden to a kohen (below 18:1), since we believe her words about herself, and the betrothed is not believed about her.
and if she married a kohen she need not leave. According to her words she is not a prostitute, as she had no forbidden relations.
they murmur about her... and with other men. She was suspected, during her betrothal, of having relations with her betrothed and with others.
even though her betrothed came to her in his father-in-law's house. It is possible to attribute the pregnancy to him, and the child will be fit.
just as she abandoned herself to her betrothed. Just as she had forbidden relations with her betrothed (see Hilchot Ishut 10:1), we must be concerned that she was also licentious with others.
as we explained. In the previous halachah.
he is not from my husband. And he is therefore a mamzer.
presumed fit. There is no flaw in his status.
for the Torah believed only the father. As above in halachot 15-16.
whose husband was overseas. And there is apparent support for her words.
presumed a mamzer. And we are strict, as long as the father does not explicitly testify that the son is a mamzer (compare above halachah 16).
"I became pregnant by a gentile or a slave," the child is fit. For a child of a gentile or slave is not a mamzer (above halachah 3).
for the husband cannot deny her. Because he does not know.

when a rumor went out about her... they murmur about her. She was suspected of licentiousness.
for most relations are with the husband. We assume that the children are his, by the halachic rule that we follow the majority.
to marry her daughter in the first instance. And there is no concern that she is a mamzeret.
we are concerned for her as a prostitute. Because of the rumor, and she is forbidden to a kohen (below 18:1).
they made a stringency regarding lineage. They were strict in laws touching family lineage (see above 13:10, below 18:14).
a definite mamzer may marry a definite mamzeret. For both are outside the congregation of the Lord.
is forbidden to marry an Israelite woman. Because of the stringency regarding lineage, to treat him as a mamzer.

and a rabbinic mamzer is permitted, etc.. They are not doubtful cases but are considered mamzerim by rabbinic enactment (see above halachah 10).
are forbidden to marry one another. Perhaps one of them is a mamzer and the other fit.

and if they married, they do not remain together but must divorce. For this is not a doubt but a rabbinic prohibition.
that they marry from among converts. Who are permitted both to a mamzer and to an Israelite (see above halachah 7, below 19:11).
the child is a shetuki or asufi. Whose defect is greater than that of a convert or freed slave, who are not forbidden in the congregation.
of doubtful gentile status regarding lineage. They were strict in considering him a doubtful gentile, even if most of the city is Israelite, because of the stringency they made regarding lineage.
she requires a get out of doubt. Perhaps he is an Israelite, and his betrothal takes effect.
whoever killed him is not killed for it. For one is not liable to death for killing a gentile (Hilchot Rotzeach 2:11), and this asufi is a doubtful gentile.
the court immersed him. While he was a minor (above 13:7).
like the other asufim found in Israelite cities. Who are doubtful mamzerim (above halachah 14).

we return his lost item. For we treat him as an Israelite. And there is no commandment to return a lost item to gentiles (Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 11:3).
half and half. Half of the city Israelite and half gentile.
it is a commandment to keep him alive. To care for his life and support him with charity.
and we clear the rubble from on him. We remove a collapse of stones that fell on him (see Hilchot Shabbat 2:20-21).
